newsitem.title: USA: Strong dollar worries Wall Street but rally goes on.
newsitem.headline: Strong dollar worries Wall Street but rally goes on.

text.p: The Fearful Freddies are again roaming Wall Street, warning the strong dollar will cut the earnings of U.S. multinational companies but the concern failed to rattle the stock market, as the Dow Jones industrial average roared past 7,000 points for the first time.

Investors were mesmerised this week with the stock market, and they shrugged off the possible danger that the fast-rising dollar might eat into the profits of export-oriented firms, spoiling the earnings growth that has fuelled one of the greatest bull market.
The market seemed to agree with some experts that Corporate America has the muscles to fight off any serious threat to its earnings.

The bullish concensus powered the blue-chip Dow index through another milestone high of 7,000 points, just four months after it breezed through 6,000 in October of last year. In late trading Friday, the Dow was off 22.71 points at 6,999.73 as it paused to catch its breath.
The dollar has been rolling higher since the second quarter of 1995, having soared more than 55 percent to 124 Japanese yen and climbing some 25 percent against the German mark to 1.68 marks.
But for multinational companies, the rise in the dollar has made it tougher for them to sell their goods overseas.

The risk for the stock market is that a downturn in earnings for corporate giants such as International Business Machines Corp., Ford Motor Co., Philip Morris Cos., General Motors Corp., General Electric Co. and Coca-Cola Co., could sour investors' taste for equities.
The rosy profit picture of the last couple of years has partly been rooted in strong overseas sales.

Several Wall Street brokerage firms this week put out yellow warnings flags, telling their clients that the strong dollar will weaken the companies' competitiveness overseas, which would hurt their revenues.

Other analysts, however, believe that the multinational companies will be able to stand up to the earnings test, as they reap the rewards from a strong U.S. economy and their global diversification that has given their products worldwide exposure.
Greg Smith, chief investment strategist at Prudential Securities says that the globally nimble companies should continue to post "very good" earnings this year.

"Increasingly, companies that are going to provide the earnings growth that investors expect must be successful in the global economy," he said. "Accordingly, we should expect the good earnings stories to come increasingly from multinational companies -- even despite currency changes, within reason."

The outlook is for continued dollar gains, despite a plea last weekend by the Group of Seven industrialised countries -- Germany, Japan, France, Italy, Canada, Britain and the United States -- for restraint on the U.S. currency's rise.
Stephen Roach, chief economist at Morgan Stanley, said the dollar has not moved up far enough to be a serious threat to the country's export.
"The dollar is still cheap on a trade-weighted basis," he said. "We haven't reached the point where the dollar is affecting our ability to penetrate markets abroad."

Roach said the 50 percent leap in the dollar against the yen will certainly make it "dicey" for U.S. carmakers to do business in Japan but against a much broader trade-weighted basket of 19 currencies, the dollar has moved up just 13 percent over the last 10 years and is still below the highs hit earlier in the 1990s.
"Contrary to widespread perceptions, the U.S. dollar should not be viewed a strong currency ... it is not expensive on a fundamental basis," Roach said.
He said that over the last decade, the dollar has experienced similar strong rallies, and "yet on each occasion, exports never flinched."
The high technology companies are believed to be the most vulnerable to the dollar's strength, but even that sector of the stock market is expected to tough out the currency ride.

"Export of commodity type products will be affected by a strong dollar but a lot of products exported by the U.S. are proprietary, like Microsoft software," says Jack Shaughnessy, director of research for Advest Inc., in Hartford, Conn. "Pricing for those is relatively inelastic and so there really shouldn't be a major loss of business."
